slots.text: Most founders validate ideas by asking 'would you use this?' Wrong question. Ask 'how do you solve this problem today?' Then shut up and listen to the workarounds.

Signs your user interviews are garbage:
1. You're explaining your idea upfront
2. They're giving you feature requests
3. You leave feeling validated
4. No one mentioned money
The AI wrapper trap is real. Everyone's building the same ChatGPT integration thinking it's a moat. The value isn't in the AI - it's in the workflow you're actually fixing.
Watched 3 demos this week where founders spent 10 minutes showing features that solve problems users don't have. The best products feel obvious in hindsight.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes it's the feature. Venmo adding social friction to payments created the product. Know which friction to remove vs embrace.

What actually kills early ideas:
1. Building before talking to anyone
2. Talking to the wrong people
3. Asking leading questions
4. Ignoring what they actually pay for today
Most founders skip idea validation because they think it means building surveys. Real validation is watching someone actually try to solve the problem you think you're solving.

User interviews that actually matter:

1. Ask about their current broken process
2. Watch them show you how they do it today
3. Ask what they've already tried
4. Listen for the words they use to describe the pain
The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech. It's that most workflows aren't actually broken enough to justify the cognitive overhead of learning a new AI-powered solution.
When founders say 'we need to remove friction' they usually mean 'we need to remove steps.' But sometimes the steps are there for good reasons that users actually value.
Talking to users feels awkward until you realize they want to complain about their problems more than you want to hear about them.

Signs you're automating the wrong thing:

1. Users keep asking for manual overrides
2. The 'streamlined' version takes more clicks
3. You spend more time explaining it than they spend using it
Most founders skip the boring part of idea validation: actually calculating if enough people will pay enough money. Math beats enthusiasm every time.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm what you want to hear
2. Talking to people who are too polite to be honest
3. Asking about hypotheticals instead of past behavior
The AI tooling paradox: we can build features faster than ever, but we're also building the wrong things faster than ever. Speed without direction is just expensive wandering.
Companies that obsess over removing friction from their own workflows rarely do the same for their customers. Internal productivity theater while users struggle with basic tasks.
Talking to users isn't about validating your idea. It's about understanding their actual workflow well enough to know where you fit. Big difference.

Signs your validation process is broken:

1. Everyone loves your idea but nobody pays
2. You keep changing the target customer
3. Your demo gets more complex each week
4. You avoid pricing conversations
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing 'no.' But getting 100 nos is infinitely more valuable than getting 3 polite maybes.

User interviews that actually work:
1. Ask about their current workflow, not your solution
2. Focus on their biggest frustrations
3. Listen for what they've already tried
4. Note what they pay for vs what they build themselves
5. End with introductions to similar people

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the tech - it's figuring out where humans actually want to hand over control. Users say they want automation but their behavior shows they want oversight. This tension is where most AI products die.
Workflow friction reveals itself in the workarounds. When someone has a 47-step process in Notion to do something that should take 2 clicks, that's not user dedication - that's a product opportunity.
Talking to users gets easier when you stop trying to validate your idea and start trying to understand their world. The validation happens naturally after that.

Signs you're removing real friction:
1. Users ask when it'll be ready before you finish explaining
2. They offer to pay for a prototype
3. They start explaining your value prop better than you do
4. They introduce you to their whole team unprompted

Most founders skip validation because they think they already know their users. Then spend 6 months building something nobody wants. The ego hit from being wrong early is nothing compared to the ego hit from failing publicly.

3 signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask when it'll be ready but won't pay now
3. They suggest features that sound nothing like your vision

You want skeptics who have the problem, not fans who like you.
AI tools work best when you give them terrible first drafts to improve, not blank pages to fill. Same reason rubber duck debugging works. The act of articulating the problem is half the solution.

Workflow automation always sounds good in theory. But most manual processes exist because they handle edge cases that are impossible to predict upfront. You automate the happy path and create 10x more work when things break.
User interviews where people tell you what they want are useless. User interviews where people show you what they actually do are gold. Stop asking hypotheticals. Start watching real behavior.

4 friction points that kill adoption:

1. Making people create accounts before they see value
2. Asking for data they don't have handy
3. Changing their existing workflow too much
4. Requiring them to convince their team

Fix these before adding features.
Most founders skip the boring part of validation: asking the same question 50 different ways. But that's where you find out if people actually have the problem or just think they should.

Things that kill user interviews:
1. Leading questions that confirm your bias
2. Talking to friends who won't hurt your feelings
3. Asking what they want instead of what they do
4. Taking notes during instead of recording

The AI wrapper problem is real but misunderstood. It's not that wrapping AI is bad - it's that most people wrap the wrong layer. They automate the output when they should automate the input preparation.
Watched 12 demos this month. The ones that felt magical all had the same thing: they eliminated a step you didn't know was optional. The forgettable ones just made existing steps slightly faster.
Friction isn't always the enemy. Sometimes friction is the only thing preventing your users from making expensive mistakes. Remove the wrong friction and you kill the value prop.

Signs your idea validation is actually just procrastination:
1. You're on interview #47
2. You keep finding 'one more segment' to talk to
3. You know exactly what to build but keep asking anyway
Most founders think user interviews are about asking what people want. They're actually about watching where people get stuck when they try to explain their current process.

Three things that kill idea validation:

1. Asking hypotheticals instead of digging into last week
2. Talking to people who agree with you by default
3. Confusing polite interest with actual pain

The hardest part of building with AI isn't the technical integration. It's figuring out which parts of your workflow actually need to be intelligent vs which parts just need to be fast and predictable.
When someone says your idea is 'interesting' in a user interview, they're usually trying to be helpful. When they start asking about pricing and timelines unprompted, they have a real problem.
Removing friction sounds simple until you realize that some friction is load-bearing. Users often need the pause between steps to think or context-switch.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They have unlimited budgets for everything
2. They've never heard of your competitors
3. They describe their problems in your exact terminology
4. They love all your ideas
